THE BELLRING — CUPS TODAY
COPPER · SILVER · GOLD · SUNSTEEL
Champion: VALKA THE UNDEFEATED (41–0)
The management patches all contenders. The management is not liable for pride.
The fountain. Its water arcs up and hangs at the top of the arc, glittering, and does not come down.
The Cathedral doors are painted on. There is no inside. He never went in that day.
The Grand Lantern, humming oddly in the heat. Its light is the color of honey. It will fail tonight. It never gets to.
A cherry tree in full bloom. Petals fall from it constantly, turning in the air — and never land.
The river doesn\'t flow. It glitters in place, every ripple exactly where it was.
The vanity. A hairbrush with long black hairs in it, and a jar of ribbons, white and gold.
Lysa\'s bed. Under the pillow, a list in a child\'s hand: THINGS TO DO WHEN I AM GROWN UP. The list is very long.
Picture books. One is open to a drawing of an animal with a glossy black coat. Under it, in careful letters: SABLE.
A shelf of paper stars, each with a wish written inside. Most of them are about fireworks.
A statue of the Hierophant, arms open, smiling. Someone has left a child\'s shoe at its feet. Then another. Then hundreds.
A statue of a little girl in a festival dress, holding a ribbon. There is no name on the plinth.
The pilgrims\' fire. Nobody needs it for warmth up here. They keep it lit so there is something that changes.
Clock-cases, floor to ceiling. Each face is painted with the same summer sky. Each one has stopped at noon.
A clock with a child\'s drawing tucked into its glass: a girl, a boy, a big yellow sun, and the word ALWAYS.
The Noon Gate. Warm air breathes through it, smelling of honey and cut grass.
THE HALCYON — Capt. C. Ashe.\nGangplank. Mind the gap. The gap is the whole sky.
The bow cuts through cloud the color of a bruise. Below: nothing at all, for a very long way.
The mainmast. Someone has carved PIP into it at a height that suggests standing on a barrel. Below it, smaller: CORVIN SAYS NO.
The foremast. A patched sail, a patched patch, and a single kite tangled in the rigging.
Corvin\'s chart table. Under the charts, a small painting of a woman in a Dawnguard sky-wing coat, laughing at whoever held the brush. On the back: "H.M. — don\'t you DARE frame this." It is framed.
Corvin\'s books: "Navigation for the Reluctant," "Debts and How to Outlive Them," and a much-read book of children\'s bedtime stories with the price still on it.
Ilse\'s stove. Something is simmering. It smells like home, if home were mostly onions.
Ilse\'s shelf: bandages rolled tight, tinctures labeled in tiny exact handwriting. One jar just says: PIP. NO.
Nell\'s forge, built into the ship\'s boiler. It runs on coal, spite and, lately, the heat of a Sun Shard on a long chain.
THE KEEPER\'S HOURS\nThe sun wakes in the east. At noon it stands above us. At evening it goes home to the west.\nRing the hours as the sun walks them, and the Lantern will hear you.
A wall of glass has grown across the bridge, clear as still water and hard as a vow. Something in the garden below must open it.

A nomad\'s water barrel. On the lid, a tally scratched with a knife: one notch for every day. The notches stop on the day the sun broke. Beside them, in a child\'s hand: STILL HERE. STILL HERE. STILL HERE. Then nothing.
A caravan tent, its poles fused into the glass. Inside, a bedroll, a cold teapot and a child\'s sandal. Whoever lived here packed in a hurry and left the important things.
A Choir pilgrim, still in her traveling sandals, facing the Lantern. She came all this way to hear the Dawnsong one last time.
A wall of blue ice seals the stair. Deep inside it, the shadow of a monk\'s hand, pressed flat, as if he had tried to hold the avalanche back.
More ice. Above it, very faintly, a voice reciting the same short prayer over and over.
A cairn of stones. On the top stone, in charcoal that the snow has somehow never touched: HALVARD. A monk\'s prayer-cord is wrapped around it. Someone came back for him.
Through a cracked shutter: a monk\'s cell. A cot, a candle stub, and a table covered in drawings of a tuning fork, each with a single note crossed out.
The refectory. Forty bowls set out on a long table, forty spoons beside them. The soup froze a year ago. No one sat down.
The monastery bell lies split in the snow. It rang the hours on this mountain for six hundred years. Then it rang the avalanche.
The village well. A bucket on a rope. The water at the bottom is perfectly clear: the only clean water in Mirefen. Osk kept it that way to the end.

Through the window of the stilt-house: rows of cots, each one neatly made, each one empty. A chalkboard: NAME / HOUR / MEDICINE, filled in until the chalk ran out, then filled in with charcoal, then with a burnt stick.
A child\'s wooden boat on the windowsill, carved with more love than skill. Painted on the side: FOR MOTHER OSK, WHO MADE ME BETTER.
Osk\'s hut. Herbs hang from every beam. On the door, a list of names in her neat hand, each one crossed out, gently, with a single line.
Carved inside the hollow oak, at a child\'s height: LYSA WAS HERE. Below it, in a careful, very old hand: SO WAS ELOWEN.
A cherry tree, still in blossom. The only living thing in the court. Petals fall and do not land; they hang in the air, as if waiting to be told what to do.
A ward of raw lightning hangs across the bridge, humming like a hive. Your hair stands on end from three paces away.
A storm-rider of Stormcrown, carved in stone, arm flung up to the sky. The inscription: FLY INTO IT. Someone has added, underneath: BUT MAYBE NOT TODAY.
Another rider, younger, laughing. The sculptor caught a crack in the stone running right across the smile, and kept it.
The Stormcrown Pride, Vasha\'s flagship, broken across the rocks. Her figurehead is the Ardent herself, carved mid-shout, finger pointing at a horizon that isn\'t there.

Vasha\'s flight log, under a stone. Last entry: "Gave the Dawnstone to the Hierophant today. He held my hands and thanked me. I have never been so certain of anything." A week later, written so hard the pen tore the page: "WHAT HAVE I DONE."
The Bellwright Fountain. Dry for a year. Someone has dropped a single coin in it anyway, very recently, for luck.
A statue of the first Hierophant, arms raised to the sun. Someone has chalked a mustache on him. It is a very good mustache.
A Dawnguard cot, the blanket squared to regulation. Pinned above it: a child\'s drawing of a knight with a very large sword, signed TO DAD.
The cradle of the Great Lamp of Aurenne. The glass is cracked from rim to base. It was the brightest light in the world for nine hundred years.
The village Hearthstone. Cold, for the first time in anyone\'s memory. Someone has left a bunch of dried sea-lavender on it.
Tobias\'s shack. A note pinned under a stone in his square capitals: BACK SOON. DON\'T TOUCH THE NETS. The nets are still here. Nobody touched them.
Nana Brisa\'s house. Through the window, jars of herbs labeled in tiny exact handwriting. One just says: DO NOT. LET WREN. TOUCH.
Two plates. Two cups. A year of ash on both.
Your bed. Unmade, obviously. Some things survive the end of the world.

Your father\'s books. Sea charts, star charts, and the pirate-queen novel with the last chapter torn out. Tucked in its place, a folded paper in your mother\'s hand: "She ends up happy. Don\'t tell Wren, she\'ll want to read it herself."
Your own books, salt-stiff. The Sunward Atlas is not among them. You took it with you. You remember choosing it over a sweater.
The great lamp of Lanternfall, dark. Inside the brass, where the Dawnstone used to sleep, nothing at all. It is only a lamp now.
A Choir supply barge, sunk with its cargo: thousands of candles, still in their wrappers. Every one unlit.
An old Aurenne galleon, two hundred years down. The figurehead is a woman holding a lantern. Someone, long ago, gave her a face like a mother\'s.
A smuggler\'s sloop. In the hold, crates stamped PROPERTY OF C. ASHE — DO NOT OPEN. Corvin pretends not to see them.
A cot, made with hospital corners. A child\'s drawing is tucked under the pillow: a big woman in a hood, and the words MOTHER OSK MAKES IT STOP HURTING.
A cot, made with hospital corners. On the blanket, a single dried flower, placed very carefully.
A cairn of gray stones. On the largest, chiseled by someone who was not a mason: SIR ALDOUS VENN. HE STOOD BETWEEN.
A stone knight, sword point-down, head bowed. The plinth reads: DAME ORSOLA OF THE WESTMARCH. SHE WAS AFRAID OF HORSES.
A stone knight with a cracked shield. The plinth reads: SIR TEODOR BRAND. HE WEPT AT EVERY KNIGHTING, INCLUDING HIS OWN.
A stone knight, very young, very serious. The plinth reads: SIR ALDOUS VENN, AGE NINETEEN. Somebody has scratched underneath, much later: STILL AN IDIOT. — G.T.
The Rook Queen\'s nest: a ring of buttons, spoons, bottle caps, a brass doorknob, three wedding rings and, right in the middle, a child-sized empty space shaped like a knife.
A kite with a lopsided sun painted on it, tangled in the junk. A name on the spar in crayon: TILLY. PROPERTY OF. KEEP OFF.
The Kingfisher\'s mainmast, snapped. Her colors still fly from the stump: Dawnguard blue, with a kingfisher stitched over the sunburst by someone who could not sew.
A bow gun, still loaded. The gunner\'s gloves are on the breech, laid down neatly side by side, as if he meant to come back for them.
A small bed with a patchwork quilt. Every patch is a different shade of yellow.
A shelf of wooden animals: a gull, a cat, a lopsided horse. Carved by a twelve-year-old, badly, with enormous care.
A star chart, inked on sailcloth. Half the stars are crossed out. Beside the gaps, in tiny writing: "fell?" "fell." "FELL. Bother."
A copy of The Sunward Atlas, annotated in red ink by its own author. The margins are fuller than the pages.
A shelf of books about the sun. Every one ends with the same chapter title: "And Then It Rose Again."
Two plates. Two cups. A third chair, pushed in, that nobody has sat in for seven years.
Your father\'s books. Sea charts. Star charts. A novel about a pirate queen with the last chapter torn out.
A statue of the Hierophant as a young man, arms open. The plinth reads: HE WHO KEPT THE LIGHT. Someone has scratched underneath: AND KEPT IT. AND KEPT IT.
A statue of a girl of ten holding a book against her chest. The plinth has no name on it. It doesn\'t need one.
Seven sockets are set into the paving before the arch, each shaped like a jagged piece of something round.
A belfry bell, toppled and cracked. Its clapper has been removed and laid neatly beside it, like a sleeping child.
A Vesper soldier\'s helmet, half-buried in ash. Inside, a folded note: "Mira — if the sun really stops, I\'ll be home for supper forever. Save me a seat." The ink has faded to violet.
A small stone at the foot of the arch. Two names, carved by an unpracticed hand: LYSA LORNE. CASSIAN LORNE. Underneath, smaller: "Now they both know where the sun goes."
The bell tower. Its great bell hangs at the top of the swing, about to fall back and ring the hour. It has been about to for forty years.
An anvil with a half-forged sword on it, still glowing. The smith\'s hammer hangs in the air just above it.
A chalk drawing on the flagstones: the sun, with a little door drawn in its side. Underneath, in a child\'s capitals: WHERE DOES IT GO?
A child\'s white shoe, the buckle undone. It is facing the wall, as if whoever wore it walked straight on without it.
Here the old city wall is thinnest. The stones don\'t meet. Through the cracks, violet light, and a sound like the sea a long way down.
Lysa\'s ribbon, on the cobbles. When Sable reaches for it, it isn\'t there. It was never really there.
← PORT GALE · WHISPERWOLD →\nThe Gale Coast Road. Mind the cliffs. Mind the wind. Mind the cliffs in the wind.
THE WHISPERWOLD — 1 mile.\nTravelers are advised not to answer the trees.\nBy order of the Thistledown Reeve.
A cairn of sea-smoothed stones. A gull feather has been tucked between two of them, carefully.
A cairn of sea-smoothed stones, stacked with care. Someone built this to last.
A rockfall chokes the top of an old goat path down the cliff. Far below, the cove glitters.

BY ORDER OF THE LORD-COMMANDER: any person sheltering a girl of about sixteen years, black hair, pale complexion, is to report to the Dawnguard. REWARD.\n\nBelow it: LOST — GINGER CAT. ANSWERS TO "ADMIRAL". (DOES NOT ANSWER.) — Bettany, Fish Market.
PORT GALE — Harbor of the Gale Coast.\nEast: the Coast Road, the Whisperwold, Thistledown and Aurenne.
A bronze gull spouting water. Someone has knitted it a tiny hat.
An old well behind the inn. A bucket, a rope, and a great many wishes at the bottom, some of them probably about cider.
A sack of salted herring. The sack has teeth marks in it. The teeth marks are ginger.
The third barrel. It is labeled BAD CIDER — 1110 — DO NOT. Something inside it sloshes, menacingly.
A shelf of ships in bottles. One of them is a Dawnguard frigate, built upside down. Mags says it\'s "accurate".
An anvil, polished to a mirror. It has never once been used. "It\'s for atmosphere," says Tolliver.
A shelf of sailors\' knots, tied and labeled in a careful hand. Bowline. Sheet bend. Clove hitch. The bowline has been tied and untied so many times the rope is frayed white.
Pinned to the tent flap, in big careful letters: PASSWORD THIS WEEK — "THE RED SKY SLEEPS." DO NOT WRITE THIS DOWN. — T.
A seam of violet crystal runs through the quarry wall like a vein. It is cold enough to hurt, and it is breathing. Someone has been chipping it out by the cartload.
Sacks of glittering violet dust, stenciled: GENUINE SCARECROW STUFFING — 2 SILVER — KEEPS CROWS OFF FOREVER.
A tent full of stolen flour sacks, three hats, and a very confused mule.
THISTLEDOWN — Est. by people who were tired of walking.\nInn · Trading Post · The Sage (up the hill, knock loudly, duck).
The village well. A bucket on a chain, and a smell of cold stone and moss. Someone has carved "TAM WAS HERE" on the rim. Someone else has carved "WE KNOW, TAM" underneath.
Beehives, humming. One bee lands on your hand, considers you thoroughly, and leaves unimpressed.
Books the Choir tried to burn. Some of them are singed at the edges. One is titled _On the Braiding of Callings, and Why the Cathedral Is Wrong About Everything_.

A notebook of names and Crests, in a hundred different inks. The oldest pages are dated sixty years ago. Near the middle, a single line: "C. — the Keeper\'s boy. Mender, Arcanist, Cantor, Warden. Wants more. Too much more."
A cauldron of something that smells of mint, honey and righteous indignation.
EAST — AURENNE, 2 days.\nNORTH — THE OLD QUARRY (CLOSED. BY ORDER OF RED TAM. SIGNED, RED TAM.)\nWEST — THISTLEDOWN.
A barricade of stolen crates, barrels and one very surprised-looking hay cart. Painted on it: AURENNE ROAD — TOLL — ASK FOR TAM.
The Pell well. A rope, a bucket, and three generations of initials carved round the rim. The newest just says: SORRY ABOUT THE SCARECROWS.
A standing stone, carved with spirals worn almost smooth. Moss has grown into the shape of a hand.
A wall of roots, twisted together like clasped hands. Behind it, violet light pulses slowly, like breathing.
THE RINGING BELL — Rooms · Suppers · Songs.\nNo rooks.
BELLWRIGHT ARMS & SUNDRIES — swords, salves and bell-bronze buckles.
THE LANTERN QUARTER.\nResidents only after dusk. (We mean it.)
LOW TOWN.\nMind the mud. Mind your purse. Mind your business.
A fountain ringed with seven bronze lanterns. So many coins have been thrown in that the water runs copper-green.
St. Aurel, the first Keeper, holding up the first Lantern. Someone has tied a red ribbon round her wrist. Several someones, by the layers.
The Hierophant Cassian, carved in white marble. The sculptor gave him a gentler face than any statue has a right to.
Scratched into the drain-house wall at child height: four crowns, and under them, GUTTER CORT. One crown is fresh.
The river Aure, low and brown. A gull stands on a sandbar in the middle of it, looking personally betrayed.
A brass bell over the bar. A card beneath it: RING FOR SERVICE. DON\'T RING FOR FUN. WE MEAN YOU, TERRENCE.
A pot of stew big enough to bathe in. It smells of rosemary and something brown and comforting.
A bell-founder\'s anvil, cracked clean through. Oswin keeps it "for sentiment." There is a price tag on it anyway.
Ledgers going back three generations of Bellwrights. The earliest entry: ONE (1) BELL, LARGE. PAID IN GEESE.
St. Aurel, holding up the first Lantern. Carved beneath her feet: *ONE CREST · ONE LIFE · ONE LIGHT.*
A pillar carved with the Seven Lanterns, from Lanternfall in the west to Skyreach above the storm. Someone has rubbed Lanternfall\'s carving smooth with their thumb, over many years.
An armillary sphere of brass rings. Where the little golden sun should sit at its center, there is only an empty socket.
Treatises on the Dawnsong, scored and annotated in a fine hand. One spine has been read until it broke: *On the Inversion of Hymns.*
Correspondence with the Keepers, filed by Lantern. The Lanternfall folder is very thin. On top, in Ysolde\'s hand, one word: NO.
A shelf of hymnals. And one cookbook, which explains the stains.
Restricted shelves: Lantern schematics, Keepers\' confessions, and one very old, very angry letter from Lanternfall.
A tuning anvil. Forty years of bells were tuned on it. There is a dent in it shaped like a word you can\'t quite read.
A suit of Dawnguard plate on a stand, polished to a mirror. There is a notch in the breastplate, over the heart, that has never been hammered out.
A portrait: a broad, laughing knight with a ridiculous mustache, and a young woman trying very hard not to laugh with him.
The almshouse ledger, in a neat round hand. ADMITTED: forty-one. DISCHARGED: none. Beside each name, a small mark like a closed eye.
From up here you can see the whole City of Bells: the Cathedral, the Grand Lantern, and far off to the south, the brown thread of the Pilgrim Road.
A gray hooded lantern, dropped and cracked. The Sisters of Small Mercies carry ones just like it.
The names are worn almost smooth. Under every one, the same date: THE LONG NIGHT.
A family tomb: a mother, a father, and four small names in a row. Someone has left a wooden toy horse on it. It is very old.
The great bell of the old foundry, cracked from crown to lip. Whatever was ringing it wanted very badly to be heard.
A woman curled on a cot, humming. When you say hello, she says it back — in exactly your voice.
An old man counting on his fingers. He gets to nine and starts again. He has been doing it, he says, for a very long time. Or possibly since this morning.
This cell is empty, except for a pair of boots standing neatly side by side. The boots are still warm.
A cot with leather straps. The straps are child-sized.
The crucible. At the bottom, a residue like burnt sugar, and a smell like a summer afternoon.
THE PILGRIM ROAD — east to Saltglass.\nCarry water. Carry more water than that.
A pilgrims\' cairn. Every stone has a name scratched on it. Some of the names are very small, like children wrote them.
The ribs of a giant wyrm arch out of the sand like the frame of a ship nobody finished building.
The mainmast. Someone has carved a tally into it — dozens of little marks — and, at the top, a single word: STAY.
The foremast, splintered halfway up. A torn sail flaps from it like a flag of surrender. Or a very tired wave.
Cargo crates stamped with a dozen different port seals. Half of them are empty. The other half are labeled "DEFINITELY NOT CONTRABAND."
GREYSPINE PASS — Frosthollow, a day\'s climb.\nWALK SOFTLY. THE SNOW LISTENS.
QUIET WAY. Do not run. Do not shout.\nDo not sing, Brother Tolle.
QUIET WAY. The snow above has been waiting all winter. Do not give it a reason.
A shrine to the Keepers of Frosthollow. Pilgrims have tied strips of cloth to it — prayers, names, a child\'s mitten.
FROSTHOLLOW. Pilgrims welcome. Beds free.\nThe goats are not for petting. (They bite.)
The well is frozen over. Someone has chipped a hole in the ice and left a ladle beside it, the way you\'d leave a key under a mat.
A guest book. Three winters back, in a big looping hand: "Sir Aldous Venn and squire. Couldn\'t sleep. Lovely tea."
Steps cut into the ice by hand, worn down in the middle by centuries of monks\' feet. Each step has a number carved beside it. You are on step four hundred and twelve.
A little bell is carved into the wall by the Hearthstone, and under it: FOR THE ONES WHO HAD TO LEAVE IN A HURRY.
SALTGLASS — last sweet water for thirty leagues.\nThe Lantern is open to pilgrims from dawn until dusk.\nCaravans north: ask at the yard.
Master Ruel\'s furnace. The air above it wobbles like a mirage that can\'t make up its mind.
A mirror of polished saltglass. Your reflection is a half-step behind you, as if it\'s thinking things over.
A mirror of polished saltglass. In it, the Lantern\'s light looks like dawn. In the room, it looks like noon.
A shelf of maps — salt roads, caravan wells, wind patterns — all annotated in a quick, slanted hand. "J." in every corner.
A spring bubbles up through a crack in the glass. The water tastes of salt and, faintly, of thunder.
An egg of saltglass as big as a barrel. Something inside is curled up, waiting for a warmer century.
Copper pots, a wagon wheel, a child\'s wooden horse. A whole caravan\'s worth of things, polished smooth by sand.
GREYSPINE PASS — WEST.\nSomeone has scratched underneath, fresh: _CLOSED. SNOW._
A statue of a woman with a lantern, up to her knees in the fen. A string of dried frogs hangs around her neck. An offering, or a joke. In Mirefen it is hard to tell.
Gaspar\'s punt. The pole is worn smooth as bone where his hands go.
MIREFEN. Mind the gaps. Mind the water. Mind your manners.\nBy order of Mother Osk, Keeper of the Mirefen Light.
A sack of willow bark, half-boiled. Doctor Vey\'s handwriting on the label: _does nothing. try anyway._
A cauldron of something gray. It smells like hope, if hope had been left out overnight.
Mag Tiller\'s stall: eel-skin boots, reed charms, a jar labeled ROT CURE (GENUINE). The jar is empty. The label is very confident.
A rain barrel, carefully covered. Everyone in Mirefen drinks rainwater now. Nobody trusts the fen.
A pot of eel stew. Rusk swears there\'s nothing in it but eel. Rusk is not looking at you when he says it.
A shelf of books swollen fat with damp. _The Keepers of Old_, _Fen Remedies_, and a romance called _The Heron\'s Kiss_ with one page dog-eared to death.
Jars of herbs, eel-oil, dried frogs and something labeled in Osk\'s cramped hand: _DO NOT. EVER. (YES, YOU, HESK.)_
A cauldron, scrubbed clean. Somebody has been making soup every day for a woman who cannot eat it.
A statue of a Keeper, half swallowed by the bog. Her lantern is full of frogspawn. The frogs, at least, seem happy.
The Sunken Shrine. Someone kept a lamp burning here for two hundred years, until the fen rose. You can still see the soot on the stones.
A mooring post as thick as a man, scorched black on the side that faces the mountain. Lightning loves this place.
The Halcyon\'s mainmast. A tally of little lightning bolts is carved into it. Forty-one. The last one is very fresh, and very deep.
A fountain fed by rain-catchers. Coins glint at the bottom: offerings to the wind, for safe flights. There are a great many coins.
The Halcyon, nose-down in what used to be Ilka\'s shed. One mast is broken. The other is somehow holding a chicken.
Ilka\'s yard. Where the Halcyon crashed, there is a neat pile of salvaged timber labeled, in large letters, CORVIN\'S. YOU\'RE PAYING FOR THIS.
THE THORNWOOD.\nKeeper\'s grove beyond. Walk softly; the trees are listening.\n_(Underneath, newer, in charcoal: CLOSED. THORNS. DO NOT.)_
Fern\'s crates: bundles of arrows fletched with jay feathers, jars of honey, a sign reading NO HAGGLING, and under it, smaller: (a little haggling).
A statue of a Keeper, so old that her face has worn smooth. Somebody — recently — has put a crown of daisies on her head.
A blank slab, smoothed and ready. Nothing carved on it yet.
A small, newer stone, the letters cut in a careful, narrow hand you know very well: EDRIN — WHO WAS NOT A KEEPER, BUT KEPT US.
The first Keeper, worn faceless by four hundred years of damp. Fresh candle stubs at her feet. Someone comes down here often. Someone who comes down from the top.
The great lamp of Lanternfall. Its bed of brass is empty.
LANTERNFALL — Westmost Light of Solmere.\nChalked beneath, in a soldier\'s square capitals: HARMONIZATION IN PROGRESS. KEEP TO YOUR HOMES.
The village well. WREN + ILSE + THE SEA, carved years ago. Underneath, freshly scratched, the knife marks still pale: + PIP.
Your own shelf. Every book on it washed up on the beach. You used to think the sea liked you.
Your bed. Made. Mom made your bed. She never makes your bed.
Ilse\'s herb jars, labeled in her tiny, exact handwriting. Nana has kept every one of them dusted while she was away.
The kettle. Nana Brisa has had it on the boil since yesterday noon, just in case.
A crate of salted fish and a note: "MAELA — DON\'T." Below it: "I DID." Below that, newer: "TOBY — THE BOAT\'S FINE. COME IN FOR SUPPER."
A charcoal sketch pinned over the stove: three skinny boys in a rowboat, grinning. Under each, a name: EDRIN. TOBY. FEN.
The cot you have slept in for a year. Someone has patched the blanket a dozen times, with whatever was to hand. One patch is a piece of a Dawnguard flag.
A pot of soup, gently burning. It smells of ash-potato and, very faintly, of fish.
A cairn of stacked gray stones. Scratched on the flat stone at its foot: EDRIN HALLOWAY. HE\'D WANT A BETTER STONE.
A newer cairn. The stones are still sharp-edged. YSOLDE HALLOWAY. KEEPER. SHE HELD.
A little fishing boat, upright on the ash, a long way from any water. Painted on the bow: THE SEAGULL. Fennick\'s boat. It rose with the sea, and came down here, with him.
Fennick\'s garden. Ash-potatoes, a stubborn rosemary, and — tucked in a sheltered corner — one sprig of sea lavender, in a pot, carefully watered.
A practice post, hacked half through. Fennick\'s been keeping his arm in. Or keeping busy.
LANTERNFALL — Westmost Light of Solmere.\nThe chalk underneath has almost weathered away: ...ONIZATION IN PROGRE... KEEP TO YOUR HOMES.
The village well, torn up roots and all. WREN + ILSE + THE SEA + PIP. Somebody has added, in the last year, very small: COME HOME.
Your bed, still made. Your mother made it the morning she wrote the letter. Nobody has slept in it since.
The cutter\'s mast, snapped clean. A Dawnguard pennant still flutters from the stump, red and gold, very bright against the ash.

A sheet of white Choir paper, the gold sunburst at its head:
THE LAST STONE WAS GIVEN FREELY, BY THE KEEPER'S DAUGHTER OF LANTERNFALL.
— by order of His Radiance the Hierophant.
Someone has drawn a noose underneath.
Letters, pinned three deep. "MAMA — I\'M ON THE BIG ROCK. THERE\'S SOUP." "TO WHOEVER HAS MY DOG: HIS NAME IS BISCUIT."
"DAD — I KEPT THE BOAT. I KEPT IT. COME AND SEE." "To Corporal Hask, if you\'re alive: I forgive you for the thing with the goat."
"Bram — if a girl with red hair asks, tell her I\'m sorry I never wrote back." The handwriting is shaky. There\'s no name.
Maela\'s kettle. Big enough to bathe a pony in. Always full. Always gray.
The bar: a ship\'s rail laid across two barrels. A brass bell hangs over it. Nobody rings it. Nobody likes bells anymore.

A chart of the Shattered Sea, drawn on the back of a sail. Shards marked in charcoal. Most of them have notes: HOUNDS. GLASS. DON\'T. One, far to the east, just says: AURENNE? and underneath, smaller: HOSPITAL.
A man asleep under a thin blanket. A gray patch has crept up his neck like frost on a window. Gloam-rot.
The Gilded Psalm\'s mainmast, snapped off at the deck. Gold leaf still clings to it. The Choir built its ships to be looked at.
A chain-lock as big as a barrel, padlocked to the bridge. The chain runs away north, toward the Chainyard.
A second chain-lock. This chain runs south, toward the wreck of the Psalm.

ASH SQUARE NOTICES
· Water: one bucket per family. Ask Sorrel.
· Violet under the skin? The Ember Ward. NOW.
· The Undercroft is SEALED. — S.
· BOUNTY: the thing in the Reliquary. See Sorrel.
The Bellwrights\' Tenor tower, snapped off at the shoulder. Up in the ruined belfry, one great bell still hangs. It has no clapper. It sways in the ember-wind without a sound.
Saint Aurel the Tuner, patron of the Choir. Someone has knocked off her head and set a cooking pot in its place. It\'s a good pot.
Saint Lumen, holding up a lantern of stone. Underneath, scratched into the plinth: HE SAID IT WOULD BE NOON FOREVER.
Driftwood markers with names chalked on them. Some have little things left on top: a spoon, a ribbon, a single boot.
Driftwood markers with names chalked on them — and around every one, a ring of tiny gold-green shoots pushing up through the ash. Dawnmoss.
The east bridge ends in nothing. Far, far below, through the violet haze, something glitters — another shard, maybe. Maybe a whole country, falling slower than you.
A doorframe with no house behind it. Somebody has hung a wreath of wire and rag flowers on it, and swept the step.
The common soup pot. It smells of ash and onion and, faintly, of hope. Mostly ash.
A cauldron of boiling bandages. Ilse\'s labels on every jar nearby, in the same tiny, exact handwriting you remember. One says: DO NOT. EVER. — I.M.
Shelves of empty phial-racks. Someone has counted them in chalk: 2. Then the 2 is crossed out: 1.
Shelves stacked with sunsalt phials, glowing like coals. Someone has written a new number in chalk, and underlined it twice.
A broken pillar from the old chapel. Someone has carved a tally of every day since the Sundering. The count stopped at 300 and started over at 1, in a different hand.
Cages. Small ones — child-sized. Every door hangs open. Whatever was inside left, or was let out, or was used.

A drowned order of service, the ink run to violet: "VESPERS EVE. The Under-Choir shall descend to the Cistern and hold the Reflected Note until the Precentor\'s signal. Do not stop for any reason. — By order of the Hierophant."
Hymnals, swollen fat with water. One has fallen open to a page where somebody has written in the margin, very small: _I don\'t want to sing this one._
A reliquary statue of a Keeper holding up a lantern. Something large has rubbed against it so often that one side is polished to a shine.
A little statue of Saint Aurel, patron of tuners, still dry. Someone left a candle stub at her feet. It is not very old.
A pillar carved with a high-water mark from two hundred years ago. The water today is three hands higher.
A great bronze bell, sunk to its shoulder. Its rim is engraved: _I CALL THE LIVING. I MOURN THE DEAD. I BREAK THE LIGHTNING._ It has done none of these things in a year.
Vestry shelves. Choir robes hang in rows, dripping. There are exactly as many empty hooks as there are singers in the Loft.
A bellwright\'s anvil, carried all the way down here for repairs. The tools are laid out neatly, as if the smith only stepped away.
The old signal mast. Someone has carved every Kite\'s name into it, from the bottom up. The top name is PIP. Under it, smaller, somebody else has carved: BOSS.
The town kite-pole. A hundred kite-tails flap from it, one for every child the shard has lost to the wind or the raiders. They snap in the gusts like applause.
The end of the dock. Below: nothing, then haze, then more nothing. The wind tugs at your coat like it has somewhere to show you.
The ladder down to the Underhang. The Kites have chalked a warning on the top rung: DONT. (BOSS SAYS.)
A hammock with a blanket folded very neatly at the foot. A greatsword leans beside it. Scratched on the wall above, a tally of days — and beside every seventh mark, a tiny drawing of a shield.

A map of Kiteholm drawn on a sail, covered in pins and string. Every Kite has a pin. Every pin has a name. In the corner, a list in a careful child\'s hand: FOOD. WATER. SLINGSHOTS. COUNT HEADS. COUNT AGAIN.

Tucked under the map\'s corner: a folded scrap of paper. Inside, in pencil, a drawing of four tall people and two short ones on a beach. One of the tall ones has a sword. One of the short ones is holding her hand.
A statue of Baron Dask, welded from scrap, gazing nobly at nothing. A plaque reads: "THE AIR IS FREE. BREATHING IT IS NOT."
Crates of salvage stamped with the Choir\'s sunburst. The Baron does business with everyone. Everyone does business with the Baron. That is what makes him a Baron.
Chalked rankings: RUSTJAW. COG & SPROCKET (THE TWINS, NOT THE KITE). IRON MOLL. THE GALE ROC — UNDEFEATED. Underneath, someone has added: THE BARON (IN HIS DREAMS).
A rope bridge that used to go straight down to the lower shelf. The ropes have been cut — cleanly. Someone did not want company.
A kite-tail snagged on the rocks, faded almost white. Somebody\'s, once.
The split prow of a Choir galleon, driven into the rock like a nail. Gilt letters on the hull, half burned away: _VIGIL_.
A breach in the hull. Through it: the underside of the world, and wind, and a long way down.
The captain\'s shelf. Hymnals, a logbook, and a child\'s drawing of the sun, pinned up carefully. The sun has a face. It is smiling. It is not moving.
Gloam crystals grown through the deck like teeth. They hum in the same key as the lullaby.
The Gilded Gull, lying on her back like a beetle. Her lift-coil housing is empty, torn open from the inside.
A barrel of hymnals, swollen with rain into a single block of paper. The top one is open to "Rest Ye, Dawn-Bound."
A ward of crystallized light hums around the mainmast. Up close you can hear it: the hymn, over and over, the same eight bars.
The captain\'s bunk, made with corners you could cut bread with. Under the pillow: a pressed flower and a list of hymns, with "Rest Ye" underlined twice.
An ember crystal as tall as Bram. Inside it, very small, a shape like a bird with its wings spread, caught mid-flight.
A campfire of kite-sticks and chair legs. Someone has drawn a ship in the ash beside it, with a very large flag and a very small captain.
A table made from a door. The chart on it is mostly blank, with careful notes in the margins: HERE BE NOTHING. HERE TOO. HERE, POSSIBLY, SOUP.
Kite-tails and prayer-flags snap on the lines. Someone has stitched names onto them. Dozens of names. Under the newest: COME HOME.
Ox\'s anvil, scattered with clock-hands. Dozens of them, all pointing different ways.
The lift winch. A chalk tally on its housing counts the people who went down to the Boneyard this year. A second tally counts the ones who came up. The second one is shorter.
The stocks. Someone has carved, very small, into the wood: THE GOAT WAS A DOG.
A card table. The felt is worn through in exactly one place: where the dealer\'s left hand rests.
Ledgers to the ceiling, each spine labeled with a year. The newest are labeled only: AFTER.
A small statue of a woman holding scales. Someone has balanced a coin on each pan. They are perfectly level.
LANTERNFALL — Westmost Light of Solmere.\nThe Kindling: tomorrow at noon, at the Lantern.
The village well. Someone has carved WREN + ILSE + THE SEA into the stone. You remember carving it.
Your mother\'s herb garden. Rosemary, thyme, and a sea-lavender that has never once flowered.
Your father\'s books. Sea charts, star charts, a novel about a pirate queen with the last chapter torn out.
A shelf of your own books. Every one has washed ashore at some point. Most of them are still a little salty.
Two plates. There have been two plates for seven years.
Jars of dried herbs, labeled in Ilse\'s tiny, exact handwriting. One just says: DO NOT. LET WREN. TOUCH.
A cauldron of something green. It smells, generously, like the sea.
A crate of salted fish and a note: "MAELA — DON\'T." Below it, in different handwriting: "I DID."
A violet crystal, half-sunk in the rock. It is cold enough to hurt. You get the feeling it is listening.
A lamp hangs from a chain that goes up and up into the dark. The lift will not come down while the warden of this stair still stands.
A small patch of dusk, curled up on the marble. It is breathing, slowly. It is asleep.
THE NADIR LIGHT — the Eighth Lantern.\nUnderkeeper: O. Vey.\nMind the edge. The edge does not mind you.
THE ECHO COLOSSEUM\nProprietor: D. Marlow, late of Kiteholm.\nFights nightly. (It is always night.)
Steps cut into the cliff, going down into a dark so thick it looks wet. Someone has scratched beside them: 30 FLIGHTS. NO RAIL.
RANKS I–X. ONE MEMORY EACH.\nPrizes for first victories only.\nThe management is not responsible for anything you remember.
Aurenne, the night of the festival
